title: Figures vs Wilke
text:
NoteScope and method (18 November 2026)



An independent, read-only review of the PNGs that the rendered pages reference, plus the publication set in figures/. Each figure was checked against Wilke’s principles using the archived text (llm-wiki/handbooks/wilke2019fundamentals-readable.md); chapter numbers refer to that book. Two headline findings (V3, V9) were re-checked by hand. Nothing has been changed yet. These are open items.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V1. The seven visualizations appear in a different order in every figure
text:
V1. The seven visualizations appear in a different order in every figure

Severity: High (for the paper) · Principle: ch. 21 “Use one visual language across compound panels”; ch. 29 “Keep semantics consistent”; ch. 6

Problem.

Sorted by value: Task 1 accuracy, Task 2 score and the time estimates.
Fixed order with Basic first: the Likert estimate and contrast figures.
Alphabetical with Basic last: the hit/miss bars, task2-peak-ppc-figure, task2-peak-contrast-figure and the time violins.
Re-sorted inside every panel: the feedback figures.

Readers have to find each condition again in every figure.
Fix. Choose one canonical order and use it everywhere: Basic first, then the six alternatives grouped by design family. Where sorting by value tells the story (ch. 6 allows “another story-relevant criterion”), keep Basic pinned and highlighted.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V2. Text sizes are unbalanced at final size
text:
V2. Text sizes are unbalanced at final size

Severity: High (for the journal) · Principle: ch. 24 “Judge text and mark balance at final reproduction size”

Problem.

Likert figures (figures/likert_estimate_figure.png, figures/likert_contrast_figure.png): panel titles are 50 pt and y labels 40 pt, but the 1–5 and ±2 tick numbers are tiny.
Tiny tick text elsewhere: the PPC and peak-contrast figures, the time-position plots, the feedback y axes and the feedback caption.
Sizes not as coded: exports use showtext at 96 dpi on 180-dpi devices, so the point sizes in the code are not the printed sizes.

Fix.

Export at the journal column widths (about 3.5 in or 7 in).
Set real point sizes: ticks 8–9 pt, labels 9–10 pt.
Drop the dpi-ratio workaround for exports.
Add anchor labels to the rating axis (what 1 and 5 mean).

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V3. Hit/miss “most correct / most missed” frames highlight noise and ties
text:
V3. Hit/miss “most correct / most missed” frames highlight noise and ties

Severity: High · Figures: figures/task2_hits_misses_stimulus_by_vistype.png, task2_hits_misses_pattern_by_vistype.png · Principle: ch. 16 (no differences without uncertainty); ch. 4 (keep the accent for real emphasis)

Problem.

Row P3_16 (checked): every panel has 0% hits, yet Confidence intervals is framed “Most correct in row” and Basic topoplot “Most missed in row”.
Rows MMN_1 and N170_12: one “most missed” panel is framed out of several tied at 0%.
Cell sizes: cells hold n = 7–26, so these winners are mostly noise.
Pattern grid: it singles out differences such as 16% vs 12%.

Fix.

Preferred: remove the frames.
Otherwise:

name the metric (hit rate or mean score);
skip rows where the extreme value is tied;
print n or an interval.


The plotting code is in the UnfoldMakie worktree (uncertainty_project/working/task2_results/plot_task2_hits_misses.jl).

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V4. Feedback panels re-sort the visualizations in each panel
text:
V4. Feedback panels re-sort the visualizations in each panel

Severity: High · Figures: a305-intensity-theme-figure, …-general-bivariates · Principle: ch. 21 “Order panels by a logical sequence”; ch. 6 (horizontal labels)

Problem.

Every theme panel orders the visualizations differently, so Basic and the others move between panels.
The general-bivariates version also has rotated labels.

Fix.

Use one fixed x order in all panels.
Keep empty slots, so that columns line up vertically.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V5. Visualization names differ between figures
text:
V5. Visualization names differ between figures

Severity: Moderate · Principle: ch. 21 (consistency); ch. 22 (unambiguous labels)

Problem. The same visualizations appear under different names:

“Bivariate corner” and “Bivariate corners”;
“Confidence interval” and “Confidence intervals”;
“Basic” and “Basic topoplot”;
“Adjacent” and “Adjacent plots”.

In the Task 2 gradient plot, “Confidence intervals” also wraps onto two lines with a large gap.
Fix.

Use one label vector (vistype_labels) for every R figure and the Makie exports.
Use a short-name variant only where space requires it, and then use it everywhere.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V6. Basic topoplot is highlighted only in some figures
text:
V6. Basic topoplot is highlighted only in some figures

Severity: Moderate · Principle: ch. 4 “Make baseline colors recede behind highlights”; ch. 21

Problem.

The blue Basic accent appears in the accuracy, score and Likert figures.
It is missing from the time estimates, the gradient plots, the PPC figure, the peak contrasts and the hit/miss bars.

Fix. Apply the same accent to Basic in every figure that shows all seven conditions.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V7. Publication figures: 180-dpi PNG, in-figure titles and subtitles
text:
V7. Publication figures: 180-dpi PNG, in-figure titles and subtitles

Severity: Moderate (for the journal) · Figures: figures/comparison_accuracy*, detection_score*, likert_* · Principle: ch. 27 “Match vector or bitmap storage to figure complexity”, “Preserve a maximum-quality master”; ch. 22 “Give every figure one title in the location its medium expects”

Problem.

The publication figures are 180-dpi PNGs.
They carry their own titles and subtitles. One subtitle, for example, defines the CI (“Dunnett-adjusted simultaneous 95% CIs”).

Fix.

Export the ggplot figures as PDF or SVG (cairo_pdf, svglite).
Export the Makie grids as PDF, or as PNG/TIFF at 300 dpi or more.
Add a title = FALSE switch for the exports and move the CI definition into the manuscript caption.

The Sample page already works this way.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V8. No time contrast-vs-Basic figure
text:
V8. No time contrast-vs-Basic figure

Severity: Moderate · Principle: ch. 16 “Plot uncertainty for the comparison you actually want to make”; ch. 3, ch. 17 (log axes start at 1)

Problem. The time-estimate plots show intervals for levels and say they are “not for differences”. The Dunnett ratios exist only as tables.
Fix. Plot the ratios to Basic with Dunnett CIs on a log axis centred at 1.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V9. Task 2 gradient plot sorted by median, shows means
text:
V9. Task 2 gradient plot sorted by median, shows means

Severity: Moderate · Location: pages/task2.qmd:317–320 (task2_gradient_order uses arrange(median)) · Principle: ch. 6 “Order categories by a meaningful rule”

Problem. The plot shows means but is ordered by medians. Bivariate corner (0.68) therefore sits above Basic (0.70).
Fix. Sort by mean_score.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V10. One score, several names and units
text:
V10. One score, several names and units

Severity: Moderate · Principle: ch. 22 “Label quantitative axes … with variables and units”; ch. 21

Problem. The same Task 2 score is described differently in different figures:

The gradient plot is titled “Detection task accuracy”, its axis says “score”, and its values are 0–1 decimals.
The model figures say “Detection task score” and use %.
task2-peak-ppc-figure labels a difference axis “%” where “pp” is meant.

Fix. Use one name and one unit for the score, and “pp” for differences. Define the fade beyond 95% in the gradient plots, e.g. “fades from 95% to 99.9% confidence” (ch. 16).

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V11. Boxplots for 3–10 ordinal values
text:
V11. Boxplots for 3–10 ordinal values

Severity: Moderate · Principle: ch. 9 “Show observations when smoothed group shapes may overstate evidence”

Problem. The feedback figures draw boxplots for 3–10 values on a 5-point scale. A box suggests more distributional detail than the data hold.
Fix.

Show the points with a median tick.
Alternatively, use a theme × visualization matrix: diverging colour for the median intensity, with n printed in each cell (ch. 6, ch. 4).
Also:

lighten the boxed strips (ch. 23);
add a reference line at 0 (ch. 23);
enlarge the caption (ch. 24).

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V12. Hit/near-miss bars show no uncertainty
text:
V12. Hit/near-miss bars show no uncertainty

Severity: Moderate · Figure: figures/task2_hit_near_miss_by_vistype.png · Principle: ch. 16; ch. 19 (dot size)

Problem.

Some differences between bars are 2–5 pp, yet the bars carry no intervals.
The small orange and black dots on blue fills are hard to tell apart.

Fix.

Add Wilson 95% whiskers, or point the caption to the contrast models.
Set a minimum dot size, or give the dots a white halo.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V13. Country map is a choropleth of raw counts
text:
V13. Country map is a choropleth of raw counts

Severity: Moderate · Figure: country-count-map · Principle: ch. 15 “Use choropleths primarily for densities, and check area bias”

Problem. Russia, Canada, Australia, Brazil and China dominate the map visually with 1–6 participants each. Europe, at about two-thirds of the sample, is barely visible.
Fix. Use proportional symbols at the country centroids, or add a Europe inset, or drop the map in favour of the bar charts. The 6 bins and the equal-area projection are already good.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V14. Logo labels carry unequal visual weight
text:
V14. Logo labels carry unequal visual weight

Severity: Moderate · Figures: participant-characteristics-icons-figure, -icons-compact, software-reduced-logos · Principle: ch. 29 “Add distinctiveness without sacrificing quick comprehension”; ch. 4, ch. 19

Problem.

The logos differ in visual weight in ways unrelated to the data: multicolour MNE, the red BrainVision block, the dark Brainstorm block.
Some logos are harder to read than plain names (“erplab”, the R logo with an asterisk).

Fix. Keep text labels for the journal, as in the reduced figure. The logo version can stay on the web as an extra.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V15. Compact figure: nominal field on a sequential ramp
text:
V15. Compact figure: nominal field on a sequential ramp

Severity: Moderate · Figure: participant-characteristics-icons-compact, panel A · Principle: ch. 4 “Use equal-prominence colors for unordered categories”

Problem. Research field is a nominal variable, but it is coloured light to dark blue, which implies an order. Self-assessed level is ordered, so its ramp is fine.
Fix. Give field a qualitative palette, or a single colour with direct labels.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V16. Time violin: alphabetical, rotated labels, no task in title
text:
V16. Time violin: alphabetical, rotated labels, no task in title

Severity: Moderate · Figure: task1-time-violin · Principle: ch. 6 “Turn bars horizontal when category labels are long”, “Order categories by a meaningful rule”; ch. 22

Problem.

The violins are in alphabetical order.
The labels are rotated 35°.
The title does not name the task.

Fix.

Make the violins horizontal, in the canonical order (V1).
Title the plot “Comparison task”.

The log scale is already right.

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V17. Smaller issues
text:
V17. Smaller issues

Severity: Low


Time-position checks: tiny ticks, no 95% ribbon, and a linear axis for geometric means (ch. 24, ch. 16, ch. 3).
Contrast figures: the value labels (“+1 pp”, “0.0”, “+0.1”) overlap the dashed zero line (ch. 24).
Rating contrast figure: red marks “interval excludes zero” for gains and losses alike. Red reads as “bad”, and the colour is the only cue. Use a neutral accent with filled vs open points instead (ch. 20, ch. 4).
task2-peak-contrast-figure: open circles and alphabetical order (ch. 25, V1).
task2-score-distribution: the 0.01-bin histogram looks like a comb. Use an ECDF or a display per visualization (ch. 7–8).
task1-descriptive-gradient-plot: the mean labels collide with the top of the band, and “Confidence intervals” wraps with a large gap (ch. 24).
Sample, experience bar chart: Beginner → Expert runs top to bottom, while the multipanel figures put Expert on top (ch. 21).
Sample, full country and software charts: bars of different lengths carry the same “1%” label (for example 1.4% and 0.7%). Show n, or one decimal, below 2% (ch. 22).
Reduced figure: the country panel’s labels are larger than the other panels’ labels (ch. 21).
Typefaces: Makie figures use a Helvetica-like font and R figures use Lato. Set Lato in the Makie theme, and use plot_theme() instead of restating theme_classic() in each chunk (ch. 21, ch. 28).

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: V18. Orphaned figure files in pages/*_files

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: Done well
text:
Done well

Model estimates are dots with CIs on a restricted axis, not bars, and the CI type is always stated (ch. 6, ch. 16, ch. 17).
The contrast-vs-Basic plots, with simultaneous CIs and a zero line, are close to Wilke Fig. 16-8 (ch. 16, ch. 23).
Bar charts:

start at zero;
are horizontal, which suits the long labels;
are sorted by value with “Other” last.

The participant multipanel uses a shared 0–100% scale (ch. 6, ch. 17, ch. 21).
The section heading serves as the figure title on the Sample page (ch. 22).
The map uses 6 bins and an equal-area projection (ch. 15).
Time violins use a log scale, and the line is labelled as the geometric mean (ch. 3, ch. 8).
Everything is generated in code, with a cache tied to the data (ch. 28).

title: Figures vs Wilke
section: Priorities
text:
Priorities

One canonical order, one set of names, and the Basic accent everywhere (V1, V5, V6).
Re-export the publication figures at column size with balanced text, as vector files, without in-figure titles (V2, V7).
Remove or fix the hit/miss frames (V3).
Feedback figure: a fixed order across panels and no boxplots for tiny n (V4, V11).
Task 2 gradient sorted by mean, one score name and unit, and a time contrast figure (V8–V10).

title: Manuscript citation audit
text:
NoteScope and method (17 November 2026)



Every citation-bearing sentence and table cell in journal.typ (Introduction through Conclusion, including Table 1) and in supplement Tables S2 and S3 was checked against the archived sources, following llm-wiki/AGENTS.md: catalog → evidence record → raw passage, and the archived PDF wherever numbers, tables, figures or garbled extraction mattered. Bibliography integrity (missing/unused keys, metadata vs. PDF) was checked for both files. Earlier audits were re-checked against the current text: journal Table 1 (claim-audits/table-1.md), Table S2 (claim-audits/table-2.md) and Table S3.
The three high-severity manuscript findings and the two high-severity Sanyal findings below were re-verified directly against the PDFs (Mikheev Fig. 6, Petek Table 3, Sanyal Table 1). Verdicts are conservative; where the archive is silent, the item is marked Not verifiable rather than filled in.

Most important issues:

A4 (High), journal.typ:86–89. The Introduction says Allen’s 20% applies to “data with more than three features”. Allen’s “3D” graphics have exactly three variables (two independent and one dependent; Fig. 1A). The 20% is correct, but the population it describes is misstated.
A36 (Moderate), journal.typ:266–268. Perceptual studies that “identify areas with high uncertainty … accuracy and response time” are attributed to Hullman et al. (2015). That HOPs study asked people to estimate properties of 1–3 distributions, with no spatial search. The description fits Sanyal et al. (2009), which is already in refs.bib.
A41 (Moderate), journal.typ:291–292. “In ERP waveforms, uncertainty is commonly shown using error bars or shaded confidence intervals”. The three cited sources give examples (Kappenman: ±1 SEM shading, not a CI; Pernet: bootstrap 95% CI; Allen: a recommended CI band, with the typical ERP panel described as having “no portrayal of uncertainty”). None of them shows how common this practice is. Mikheev’s 40% without error bars points the other way.
A8 (Low), Table 1, Allen row. The 26 Oct audit’s single recommended wording correction (“Only 20% of audited 3D graphics portrayed uncertainty”) has still not been applied.

Most important issues: 1. B8 (Moderate) – Bernard et al. give TeulingFig3 the top category (++) for ER1–ER3 only on black backgrounds. On white backgrounds the same Table 3 excludes it (∉) for ER1 and ER3. The assessment is also measure-based, not a user study. Say this explicitly, or justify the choice if the stimuli use a light background. 2. B7 (Moderate) – Strode et al. say the corners model may require more legend consultation. They also could not blend a 4×4 (16-colour) corners palette with enough distinctness and fell back to 3×3. The manuscript uses a 5×5 (25-cell) grid and calls the model “suitable” without mentioning this caution. 3. B5 (Moderate) – The adjacent-plots attribution to the EEGVIS toolbox can’t be verified: there is no archived source. The only archived mention of EEGVIS (mikheev2024art) links it to 2D colour maps, not to side-by-side estimate/SE maps. 4. B9 (Low, Overstated) – The “broader warning that blue–violet mixtures … can be difficult to distinguish” is, in Strode et al., a comment on one specific overlay scheme (their Fig. 1), not a general warning. 5. BB1 (Low) – strode2019operationalizing has year = {2020}, but the archived PDF footer reads “Cartographic Perspectives, Number 94, 2019”, and the reference list currently prints 2020. 6. BB2 / BB18–BB19 (Low) – The Wilke ISBN does not match the archived copy (978-1-492-03108-6). The OpenAI model and Codex references are unarchived web pages, and the Codex URL points to a generic API “code generation” guide.

Most important issues:

Sanyal et al., Table S3 (High). Two lower-order rankings contradict or go beyond the paper’s Table 1 (PDF p. 7). The paper reports only significant pairwise contrasts. It gives no per-task means: Figs. 10–11 pool across tasks.

1D least-uncertain: S3 says “glyph colour ≈ surface colour > error bars”, but the paper reports that error bars beat surface colour.
1D most-uncertain: S3 says “glyph size > error bars”, but no such difference is reported.

Correll et al. 2018, E2 (High). S3 ranks VSUPs as “best-performing” in the Battleship task. The paper found no effect on mean uncertainty of placements. VSUPs avoided the most uncertain cells (KS test), but their placements carried higher average danger, i.e. lower expected value. The earlier S3 audit’s qualification (“not a universal decision advantage”) is not reflected.
Kale et al. E2 N = 150 (Moderate; Not verifiable). The archived paper does not state the E2 sample. The figure comes only from the authors’ external CSV, which is not archived, and the cell carries no source note.
Greis et al. Data = M (Moderate; Not supported by the archive). The archived paper never states whether the rainfall/forecast data were real or simulated. The M code rests on the dissertation, which is not archived.
Wainer & Francolini N (Moderate). S2 gives only “N: 16”. Experiment 2, which S3 ranks separately, used 8 returning participants. The S2 caption says separate values are shown when samples differ.
Several S3 cells overstate a winner or tie.

Correll & Gleicher E1 (Moderate): box plots tied bar charts on confidence.
Gschwandtner “E3b” (Moderate): centred error bars alone were significantly best.
Sterzik E2 (Moderate): the authors call texture, waves, contours, colour and hulls “similar”, not ordered.
Sterzik E3 (Moderate): texture ties colour on SES, and colour wins on sticks.
Kusumastuti (Moderate): the table omits that E2 practice used the ellipse display.
Scholz (Moderate): “mean rank 3.35” is actually a preference score, where 4 means most preferred.

F23. Unadjusted copies of the main comparisons with Basic

Severity: Moderate · Area: Task 1, Task 2, Hit or miss

Problem. The main results are the six comparisons of each visualization with Basic, Dunnett-adjusted (F14). Several places still showed the same six comparisons without adjustment. These copies added nothing and invited picking the smaller p value. Example: Task 1, Bivariate range vs Basic was p = .033 unadjusted but .13 adjusted.

Task 1: a “p (unadjusted)” column in the main comparison table; an “Unadjusted coefficients” sentence; unadjusted intervals, p values and a sentence in the conditional-logit sensitivity analysis.

F12. Task 1 text overstated weak effects (was U5)

Severity: High · Area: Task 1 reporting

section: F15. Rating models assumed proportional odds (was U9)
text:
F15. Rating models assumed proportional odds (was U9)

Severity: Moderate · Area: Subjective-rating models

Problem. The ordinal rating models assume proportional odds: a visualization shifts every rating step (1→2, 2→3, …) by the same amount, so its effect can be summarised by one odds ratio. Tests rejected this for all four questions (p = .011 to 3 × 10⁻⁵).
Resolution (18 Nov 2026). The Subjective page has a new section, “Model checks and sensitivity analyses”.

The page no longer interprets odds ratios. It reports model-smoothed mean ratings instead. These differ from the raw means by at most 0.08.
Sensitivity. A simpler linear model (rating ~ vistype + (1 | ID)) gives the same answer for 24 of 24 contrasts: the same intervals exclude zero.

section: F16. Rating ranking mixed different questions and overstated a leader (was U10)
text:
F16. Rating ranking mixed different questions and overstated a leader (was U10)

Severity: Moderate · Area: Subjective ratings

Problem. The overall ranking summed the mean ratings of the four questions with equal weight, although they measure different things (one is likelihood of use, F10; one was asked at a different time, F11), and neighbouring ranks were indistinguishable (e.g., Uncertainty markers 12.28 [11.62, 12.88] vs Basic 12.24 [11.70, 12.82]). The tables also highlighted a “leader” per question, e.g. Confidence intervals for comparison. But its difference from Basic (+0.18 [−0.09, 0.45]) included zero, so “no difference from Basic” was still plausible. Its differences from the other visualizations were never tested.
Resolution (18 Nov 2026).

The “Sum of mean ratings” column is removed. The page explains why: the items measure different things (F10) and were asked at different times (F11).
The “leader” highlighting is removed. Red now marks only clear differences from Basic. A difference is clear when its Dunnett-adjusted 95% interval does not include zero. Zero means “rated the same as Basic”. In the code this flag is excludes_zero. Example: Confidence intervals for comparison has +0.18 [−0.09, 0.45]. This interval includes zero, so it is no longer red.
A generated list under the figure names the contrasts that exclude zero. The page states that differences among the uncertainty visualizations were not tested, so it names no “best” visualization.

section: F18. Fixed item order in the rating questions (was U13)
text:
F18. Fixed item order in the rating questions (was U13)

Severity: Moderate (design limitation) · Area: Subjective ratings, manuscript

Problem. In every rating question the visualizations appear in the same order: Adjacent first, Basic always last. An item’s position affects its rating on its own (the first item sets a reference for the rest, attention drops towards the end, and the last item is seen in contrast to everything before it). Because every participant saw the same order, these position effects are mixed up with the visualizations and cannot be separated statistically. This matters most for Basic: it is the reference in every comparison and also the item most affected by being last.
Resolution (18 Nov 2026). This cannot be fixed after data collection, so it is reported:

a “Limitation: fixed item order” callout on the Subjective page;
the Task 3 description and a first paragraph in the Limitations section of journal.typ.

section: F20. Stale hard-coded text and suspicious items (was U15)
text:
F20. Stale hard-coded text and suspicious items (was U15)

Severity: Low · Area: Task 1 and Task 2 pages

Problem. Four unrelated small issues:

Task 2 score-distribution caption: said 2,394 scores, a number typed in at an earlier sample size; at N = 146 there were 3,066.
Task 2 random-slope note: gave a position-slope SD of 0.006 that was typed in by hand and computed by no code (a refit gave 0.013), and mentioned an alternative model that did not exist.
Task 2 estimate figure: the x-axis started at a hard-coded 0.58, just below the lowest interval (0.589), so new data could silently cut intervals off.
Task 1 items below chance (50%): target MMN_19 had 41.6% accuracy and one pair 9% (n = 11). Below-chance accuracy can mean the answer key is wrong.

Resolution (18 Nov 2026).

Task 2 score-distribution caption. The count is now generated (3,066).
Task 2 random-slope callout. The position-slope SD is now computed from a fitted (1 + position_c | ID) model: 0.013 per trial, against a fixed effect of 0.002. The unsupported claim that a diagonal visualization model “remains available” is removed.
Task 2 axes. The estimate and gradient figures take their x-ranges from the data.
Task 1 below-chance items. These are not mis-keyed: all 3,066 trials pass an answer-key consistency check. They are hard MMN targets that resemble some N170 maps. The diagnostic is a collapsed section on the Task 1 page; the follow-up is U16.

title: Fixed
section: F22. Random slopes in the rating models were not explained (was U9)
text:
F22. Random slopes in the rating models were not explained (was U9)

Severity: Low · Area: Subjective-rating models

Problem. The rating model (rating_ord ~ vistype + (1 | ID)) lets participants differ only in their overall rating level. The page did not say why participant-specific preferences for visualizations (random slopes) were left out.
Resolution (18 Nov 2026). Random slopes cannot be estimated here. Each participant rated each visualization only once per item. A participant-specific effect per visualization would rest on a single rating and cannot be told apart from ordinary noise. So the model keeps only each participant’s overall level (random intercept). The “Model checks and sensitivity analyses” section on the Subjective page explains this.

text:
U16. Two MMN targets are hard to tell from N170

Severity: Low · Area: Task 1 stimuli, manuscript

Problem. The below-chance items from F20 are not mis-keyed: every trial passes the answer-key check. MMN_19 (41.6% correct as target) and MMN_29 (45.5%) fail only against N170 distractors (15.5% and 20.5% correct), not against P3 distractors. Both are weak maps (±1.5 and ±1.7 µV) with lateral rather than posterior positivity, and some N170 variations (N170_7, N170_12, N170_16) look like the MMN template. Across all MMN targets, accuracy is 56.3% against N170 distractors and 85.8% against P3 distractors.
The hard items are spread evenly across visualizations, so they add noise rather than bias. They stay in the primary analysis.
Exploratory refit (items chosen after seeing the data): dropping the two targets moves the omnibus test from p = .056 to p = .028. The Bivariate corner and range odds ratios become 0.64 and 0.65, with Dunnett-adjusted intervals still including 1 (adjusted p = .11 and .12).

Whether the manuscript mentions the exploratory refit.
The Stimuli section should say that some single-subject MMN and N170 maps look alike.

U21. Rating models: test ignores clustering; estimates are conditional

Severity: Low · Area: pages/subjective.qmd:258–270, :321–327

Problem.

The proportional-odds test uses fixed-effects clm, which treats each participant’s 7 ratings per item as independent. Its p values (< .001 to .011) are therefore too small, so “rejects proportional odds for 4 of 4” is overstated. The conclusion (do not interpret odds ratios) is conservative and still holds.
mean.class from clmm is evaluated at a participant effect of 0. It is not a population average; it is close to the raw means (≤ 0.08) here only empirically.

Fix.

Say that the test ignores clustering, so its p values are approximate.
Label the estimates “expected rating, typical participant”.

See Gelman, Hill & Vehtari (2020), §15.5.

title: Table S3 literature audit
section: Scope and interpretation
text:
Scope and interpretation
This audit supports the criterion-specific rankings added to Supplementary Table S3. It covers the 13 empirical evaluations already listed in Supplementary Table S2. A ranking is reported only when the paper provides a point-estimate order, an inferential comparison, or an explicit author conclusion. ≈ denotes a tie, an inconclusive contrast, or no reliable difference; it does not assert numerical equality. Partial orders are retained where the paper does not support a complete ranking.
The archived PDFs were inspected for every table- or figure-based ranking. This was especially important for Sanyal et al., whose extracted text has a broken font mapping.

The evidence supports a contrast between bar charts and the symmetric alternatives, not a reliable ordering among the alternatives.

A2. Mikheev survey percentages did not exist in the paper

Severity: High · Location: journal.typ:70–73, Introduction · Fixed: 18 November 2026

Problem. The Introduction said: “In our previous survey of 213 M/EEG researchers, 52% of respondents reported having previously created topoplots. This is the second results after conventional ERP waveforms (61%) @mikheev2024art.” Neither number appears in the paper as a plotting rate. 52% occurs nowhere; the only 61% is an unrelated result (61% of 185 respondents read a topoplot series as time-point snapshots). The ranking was right.
Evidence. Figure 6 of Mikheev et al. (2024), PDF p. 9 (caption anchor, archived PDF): 175 of 213 respondents had plotted a topoplot (82%) and 187 of 213 an ERP plot (88%). These counts exist only as bar labels in the chart, so they are not in the extracted text, which is why text-based checks could not catch the error.
Fix.

The sentence now reads: “In our previous survey of 213 M/EEG researchers, 82% of respondents (175) reported having previously plotted a topoplot, second only to conventional ERP waveform plots (88%, 187) @mikheev2024art.” It carries a source comment, // Source: mikheev2024art, Fig. 6 (PDF p. 9) …, which does not print. journal.pdf was recompiled with scripts/compile-journal.ps1.
Prevention: the Figure 6 counts for all eight plot types were added to the wiki as evidence claim mikheev-plot-familiarity, noting that they must be checked against the figure. The wiki was rebuilt and validated.

section: A17. Petek: “quantifying” counted rows where tools only draw
text:
A17. Petek: “quantifying” counted rows where tools only draw

Severity: High · Location: journal.typ, Table 1, Petek et al. (2026) row · Fixed: 18 November 2026

Problem. The cell said: “For only 5 of the 18 visualizations did at least one tool provide built-in support for quantifying uncertainty. For the remaining 13 (72%), users had to construct the visual encoding themselves.” Petek et al. rate each tool on each visualization as ✓ (the tool quantifies uncertainty and draws it), ◦ (the user quantifies, the tool draws) or × (the user does both). Only 3 rows have a ✓; on 2 more the best any tool offers is ◦, so users still quantify there. “5 … quantifying” was therefore wrong, and the second sentence left out that the 13 remaining rows also need the user to quantify. The 13/18 (72%) count was correct. This error appeared after the 26 October Table 1 audit.
Evidence. Petek et al. (2026), Table 3 and its legend, PDF p. 18 (raw passage, archived PDF): ✓ rows are confidence interval for mean, point-wise confidence band around a regression line, and bar chart with confidence interval for mean; ◦-only rows are uncertain binary heat map and uncertain bivariate means; the other 13 rows are × for all five tools.
Fix. The cell now reads: “Only 3 of the 18 visualizations had a tool that both quantified and drew the uncertainty; for 2 more, tools drew it but users had to quantify it. For the remaining 13 (72%), users had to do both themselves.” A source comment with the row counts sits under the cell and does not print. journal.pdf was recompiled with scripts/compile-journal.ps1; the rendered table was checked.
